response_text: In this lab, the fundamental OS clock was configured to tick every 1 millisecond, meaning the operating system checks and handles timing-related events at that interval. If we were to reduce the clock period to 0.1 milliseconds, one potential benefit would be improved responsiveness and finer timing resolution. Threads could be scheduled with greater precision, and the OS could react to events more quickly, which may be useful for applications requiring real-time behavior with tight timing constraints. However, a shorter tick interval significantly increases the number of interrupts the processor must handle per second, introducing considerable overhead. This frequent interruption can degrade overall system performance, as the CPU spends more time servicing SysTick interrupts and less time executing useful thread work. The increased context-switching frequency can also lead to stack overflows and timing issues if the system is not designed to handle such high rates. Therefore, while a 0.1 ms OS clock could offer better timing granularity, it would also reduce efficiency and reliability.\n
